chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Trade Wars Move Markets

lessons.title: Sector Impact: Winners and Losers in Indian Equities

children.text: "Trade war hits Indian markets" is a headline, not an analysis. A trade war does not hit the Nifty as one block, it hits specific sectors, in specific ways, some of them directly and some of them through second- and third-order effects that take longer to show up in earnings. This lesson breaks Indian equities into four buckets: direct losers, carved-out sectors, indirect losers, and surprising winners.
Direct Losers: Sectors Sitting in the Tariff's Path

Some sectors are named explicitly in the tariff order. India's 2025 experience made this obvious: textiles and apparel, gems and jewellery, and shrimp and seafood were among the categories hit hardest by the 50% US tariff, precisely because the US is such a large buyer for each of them. These are labor-intensive, export-dependent industries centered on hubs like Surat (diamonds and jewellery), Tiruppur (knitwear), and coastal Andhra Pradesh (shrimp), where a large share of output is built specifically for the US market.

children.text: The Carve-Outs: Why Pharma and Electronics Mostly Dodged It

markDefs.definition: A specific product category deliberately excluded from a broader tariff order, typically because the importing country considers continued cheap access to it more important than the protectionist goal, such as affordable medicines or critical electronics components.

children.text: Not every export got caught in the 2025 tariff. Generic pharmaceuticals and most electronics, including smartphones, were largely spared through explicit

. The logic is straightforward: the US relies heavily on Indian generic drug makers for affordable medicines, and disrupting that supply creates a domestic political problem worse than the one the tariff is trying to solve. Electronics exemptions similarly reflect how embedded global electronics supply chains have become; taxing your own consumer electronics supply is a strange way to win a trade war. This is why Indian pharma majors and IT hardware-adjacent names were comparatively insulated from the direct hit that textile and jewellery exporters took.

body.title: Want the detail? A closer look at how carve-outs typically get decided

children.text: Carve-outs are usually justified on one of three grounds: essential goods (medicines, food, energy), embedded supply chains (electronics components no single country can quickly replace), or reciprocal leverage (holding a category back as a bargaining chip for future negotiation rather than taxing it immediately).

content.text: Carve-out lists are not permanent. They get revised as negotiations continue, so treat any specific exemption as a snapshot, not a guarantee, and confirm the current tariff schedule before making an investment decision based on it.

children.text: IT services is the clearest example of a sector that is not directly tariffed but still gets hit. Software and consulting services generally fall outside goods tariffs altogether. But Indian IT majors earn a large share of revenue from US clients in manufacturing, retail, and automotive, sectors that are themselves absorbing tariff costs and tend to freeze discretionary technology spending when their own margins are under pressure. The tariff never touches the IT company's invoice directly; it touches the client's budget first, and the IT company feels it a quarter or two later in slower deal signings, not in a tariff line item.
The Surprising Winners: Trade Diversion and China Plus One

Trade wars create both losers and winners even within the same broad sector, depending on which side of the shift a company sits on. When a major market shuts its door to Chinese goods, that Chinese production has to go somewhere, and it often gets redirected, at discounted prices, toward markets that stayed open, India included. Indian steel producers have repeatedly had to seek anti-dumping duties against cheap Chinese steel finding its way into the Indian market during periods when China's traditional export markets tightened. That is a loss dressed up as a domestic industry problem, not a trade war win. On the other side, specialty chemicals and auto component makers have genuinely gained as global buyers diversify sourcing away from a China-only supply chain, a slower-moving but more durable version of the China Plus One theme you saw in Chapter 1.

body.title: Direct, Indirect, or Diversion?
body.question: A US retailer tells its Indian IT vendor it is pausing a planned technology upgrade because its own imported inventory costs have risen sharply. Which bucket does the IT vendor's revenue hit fall into?
body.explanation: The IT vendor is not tariffed itself, services generally are not. The hit arrives through its client's budget, one step removed from the tariff, which is the definition of an indirect, second-order effect.

body.text: Sector-level conclusions are a starting point, not a stock pick. Within "textiles" or "specialty chemicals," individual companies can have very different US revenue exposure. Check a specific company's export mix and geographic revenue breakup, screener.in's export ratio and peer comparison tools are a reasonable starting point, before assuming a sector-wide trend applies to the stock you are looking at.

A trade war sorts Indian equities into four groups, not two: sectors it hits directly, sectors it carves out, sectors it hits indirectly through their clients, and sectors that quietly win as trade gets redirected around the fight. Most investors only ever look for the first group.

points: Direct losers are named explicitly in tariff orders: India's 2025 experience hit textiles, gems and jewellery, and seafood hardest, since the US is a dominant buyer for each.
Carve-outs (pharma, most electronics) reflect the importing country protecting its own supply of essentials, not goodwill toward the exporter, and can be revised as negotiations continue.
Indirect losers, like IT services, are not tariffed themselves but absorb the hit a quarter or two later, through client budgets tightening.

Trade diversion can turn a sector into a quiet loser (steel facing redirected Chinese supply) while supply chain diversification turns another into a quiet winner (specialty chemicals, auto components).
Sector-level analysis is a starting point. Always check a specific company's actual US revenue exposure before assuming the sector story applies to it.
